g3ela-23-1-teach-morph: [curious] Have you ever walked across a bridge? You start on one side and end up on the other. There's a word part that means across. Trans. T, r, a, n, s. Trans, plus Pacific, makes transpacific: across the Pacific Ocean. But careful! Tranquil starts with t, r, a, n, and it just means calm. Nothing goes across. Read the three words, and think about the questions. Then tap See if you cracked it, and type the missing parts.
g3ela-23-1-teach-vocab: Let's be word detectives with a word that's not in your bank. Chamber. Here's a sentence. The lord slept in a small chamber at the top of the tower. He slept in it, so a chamber must be a room. One, read the sentence. Two, look for word parts. Three, check that the meaning fits. Fill in each sentence with a word from the bank, and tap Check My Work. Then play the matching game.
g3ela-23-1-teach-gram: [warmly] Some words are names, and names get capital letters. Listen. Stories say Robin Hood lived in Sherwood Forest. Robin Hood names a person. Sherwood Forest names a place. Every important word in a name gets a capital. A book title does too, like The Wind in the Willows. But little words inside, like in and the, stay small. Tap Now check your thinking. Then sort each name: a person, a place, or a title.
g3ela-23-1-teach-spell: Watch me split a long word. Puppet. Find the vowels: u, and e. In between sit two consonants, p and p. Vowel, consonant, consonant, vowel. That's V C C V! So I split right between the two consonants. Pup. Pet. Say the words in Group A and Group B out loud, and tap See the Rule. Then sort all eight words.
g3ela-23-2-teach-morph: Remember, trans means across. Here's a long one that's not on your list. Transcontinental. Find trans at the front. A continent is a giant piece of land. So a transcontinental train goes all the way across it! Read the Remember box. Then tap a word, and tap what it means. Match all four words.
g3ela-23-2-teach-vocab: Here's a word from the world of trades. Guild. A guild was a club for one kind of worker, like all the bakers in a town. Read each sentence with a bank word in the blank. If it makes sense, keep it. Then play the matching game.
g3ela-23-2-teach-gram: Spot the capitals with me. abbot peter walked to bath abbey. Abbot starts the sentence, and it's his title. Peter is his name. Bath Abbey is a place, so both words get capitals. That's four! Read the Remember box. Then tap every word that needs a capital.
g3ela-23-2-teach-spell: Use your eyes for this one. Sofa. Pony. Doctor. Which one has two consonants between its vowels? Doctor! O, then c and t, then o. Doc. Tor. Read the rule. Then in each row, tap the one word with two consonants in the middle.
g3ela-23-2-teach-rwm: [warmly] Let's try all three parts with a different sentence from today's article. Poor children worked in the fields or served in the homes of nobles. Part one, read like a reader. Poor children had jobs, in the fields or in a noble's home. Part two, read like a writer. The little word or joins two choices, and both halves have the same shape: worked in, served in. Part three, mimic. Here's mine: Opti worked in the library or perched in the old oak. Now it's your turn with the apprentice sentence. Write one sentence in each box.
g3ela-23-3-teach-morph: Let's build one together. Trans. It. Push them together: transit! Transit means going across, from one place to another, like a bus ride across town. Say each pair of parts out loud. Type the whole word in the box. Then tap Check My Answers.
g3ela-23-3-teach-vocab: At court, people called the king Your Majesty. Majesty is a word for the greatness of a king or queen. Saying it showed respect. Read how we figured out the first word. Then fill in each sentence with a word from the word bank, and tap Check My Work. Last, play the matching game.
g3ela-23-3-teach-gram: Count with me. earl roger sailed to ireland. Earl starts the sentence, and it's his title. One. Roger is his name. Two. Ireland is a place. Three. Sailed and to aren't names, so they stay small. Read the Remember box. Then count the capitals in each sentence, and type the number.
g3ela-23-3-teach-spell: Oops. I split garlic like this: ga, rlic. That sounds wrong! The two consonants in the middle are r and l. Split between them. Gar. Lic. Garlic! Read the rule. Then tap each word to split it between its two middle consonants.
g3ela-23-4-teach-morph: Riddle time. I come at the front of a word. I have five letters. And I mean across. What am I? Trans! Try this one. Transcribe. To write across, copying words from one place to another. Tap Roll the Dice. Say what each word means, and tap Check My Thinking. Roll all six.
g3ela-23-4-teach-vocab: One more food word before you go. Trencher. The article says some people ate from thick slices of bread called trenchers. A plate you could eat! Read each sentence with a bank word in the blank. If it makes sense, keep it. Then play the matching game.
g3ela-23-4-teach-gram: Something looks funny here. We saw a Castle on the hill. Castle has a capital, but it isn't the name of one castle. It could be any castle! So it stays small. Read each sentence out loud. Tap the word that's wrong, or tap No mistake.
g3ela-23-4-teach-spell: Roll one with me. Window! The vowels are i and o. In the middle sit n and w. Split between them. Win. Dow. Tap Roll the dice. Say the word out loud and split it into syllables. Then tap Check my answer. Roll all six words.
